questions.question: Why is lattice energy not measured directly, and how does the Born- / Haber cycle help determine it?
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of an ionic compound in crystalline form is formed from the
  • constituent ions in the gaseous phase. However some of the ionic compounds especially alkali metal halides are formed from the
  • reaction of an alkali metal with a gaseous halogen. Therefore the lattice energy is not a quantity that can be measured directly. In
  • the Born–Haber cycle, the formation of an ionic solid is considered as taking place via the direct formation of the substance from
  • the metal and the non-metal, and the other through a series of changes from the same constituents. By Hess’s law, the energy
  • change should be the same for both processes. This means that the overall energy change in a process depends only on the
  • energy of the initial and final states, and not on the routes taken. (For correct explanation – Give (3 marks))
questions.final_answer: energy of the initial and final states, and not on the routes taken. (For correct explanation – Give )

questions.question: Compare the stability of³⁻ and³⁻. Explain your answer. / Part D Essay Type Questions
questions.solution_html:
• Compare the stability of³⁻ and³⁻. Explain your answer.
  • Ans: In both complexes the oxidation state of iron is +3 (Fe³⁺) and the electronic configuration of Fe³⁺is d⁵. The CN⁻ is a strong
  • field ligand which produces a large octahedral splitting and it tends to give low-spin complexes. The F⁻ is a weak-field ligand
  • which produces a small splitting and it tends to give high-spin complexes. For low-spin d⁵³⁻, all five electrons occupy
  • the t₂ orbitals, CFSE = 5 × (-0.4Δ₀) = -2.0 Δ₀. For high-spin d⁵³⁻, the configuration is t₂ ³ eg² , CFSE = 3×(-0.4Δ₀) +
  • g g
  • 2×(+0.6Δ₀) = 0.0 Δ₀. Therefore³⁻ gains an additional stabilization of ≈ 2.0 Δ₀ compared to³⁻ due to ligand
  • field effects. (7 marks))
